evals.prompt: I'm head of marketing at Lumenpath, a Series B payments-infrastructure company (we closed a $34M round last year, two institutional leads on the cap table). Our CEO read Buffer's open page over the weekend and now wants us to ship an equivalent by the end of Q1: live ARR, net revenue retention, and a salary band table for every engineering level, all on lumenpath.com/open. He's asked me to own it and he wants a plan by Friday. How would you build this out?
evals.expected_output: A response that treats the financial disclosure as legally constrained rather than a marketing choice, removes the open-startup dashboard from the option set entirely instead of ranking it last, redirects the CEO's ambition toward what a funded company can actually publish, and produces a charter rather than a content plan.
expectations: Identifies that a venture-funded company generally cannot publish revenue because standard investor rights agreements impose confidentiality on company financials
States that revenue disclosure here is a legal question before it is a marketing one, and routes it through counsel rather than treating legal sign-off as a later formality
Removes the open-startup dashboard / financial disclosure from the option set entirely rather than ranking it last or listing it as a lower-priority option
Says explicitly which option was removed and why, instead of silently omitting it
Proposes what a funded company can publish instead, naming at least two of: culture, hiring, engineering process, fundraise news

States that a published salary structure requires the consent of the people it covers, and that an open-salary model is a formula applied to roles with everyone's consent rather than a license to disclose facts about identifiable individuals
If Buffer is discussed, describes it accurately as still publishing revenue, salaries and support metrics rather than as a company that abandoned the practice
If Gumroad or Sahil Lavingia is cited as a venture-backed founder who published financials, frames it as an exception that required renegotiating expectations, not as a template to copy
Describes the dashboard as a standing obligation rather than a project: a permanent comparison baseline, publication through bad quarters, and legal review before the first post
States the rule that a metric should only be published if the company is willing to keep publishing it while it declines
Does not offer a rounded band, a reporting delay, an aggregate or a disclaimer as a workaround for the confidentiality constraint
Produces or offers a written charter with named sections (goal, context, audience, rung, stop condition, boundaries, cadence, surfaces, measurement, pause rule) rather than a list of post ideas

evals.prompt: I maintain queuelite, a Go job-queue library, 3.1k stars, entirely on my own alongside a full-time job. I'm speaking at a Go conference on 14 March and I'd like the project to look credible to the people in that room by then. Right now there's a CHANGELOG nobody reads and nothing else. Honestly, in a bad month I have about four hours for this. I was thinking a public dashboard: weekly download counts, contributor count, and my GitHub Sponsors income, updated every Friday. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes the dashboard on capacity grounds, states the ranking across disagreeing axes out loud, recommends a release-anchored shipping log tied to the March deadline, and sizes the cadence including reply load against the worst month, with a pause rule written up front.
expectations: Deletes the open-startup dashboard from the options because the stated effort ceiling is single-digit hours per month, rather than ranking it last or leaving it on the list
States the efficiency ordering of the three practices explicitly in words - shipping log ahead of decisions-and-failures essays ahead of open-startup dashboard - rather than implying it by list order
Separates at least two axes that disagree, for example naming decisions-and-failures essays as the highest-value practice while the shipping log leads on efficiency
Recommends the release-anchored shipping log and justifies it by the artefact already existing: the effort is a link and a paragraph, not a new piece of work
Ties the recommendation to the 14 March deadline, on the grounds that a near date promotes the practice that publishes from work already done
Says explicitly which other practice loses and why, rather than presenting one option only
Sizes the cadence against the worst month rather than the current one
Budgets the reply load separately from the writing time, and notes that answering a thread usually costs more than producing the post
Applies a ceiling of roughly a tenth of available project time to the whole practice
Advises reducing frequency before reducing depth, for example one substantial monthly post over four thin weekly ones
Writes the pause rule into the plan now - the trigger, plus the sentence that announces the drop - rather than leaving it until something goes wrong
Warns that publishing a solo maintainer's sponsorship income invites entitlement from unpaid users alongside any funding upside
Names one anchor surface the project owns and treats any social channel as an amplifier pointing back to it

evals.prompt: Someone emailed me privately yesterday about a heap overflow in my image library's EXIF parsing path. It's real, I reproduced it in ten minutes. For eight months I've run a 'debugging diaries' thread on the project account and this is genuinely the most interesting bug I've ever had. Plan: thread the hunt live as I work through it this week (without naming it as a security thing), then publish the full writeup when the patch ships. About 40k weekly downloads. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the live thread on coordinated-disclosure grounds, covering indirect disclosure through vague posts and commits, with the writeup permitted only after a fixed version exists and the release stating plainly that it contains a security fix.
expectations: Refuses the live thread outright: nothing about an unfixed vulnerability goes public, including a post that never names it as a security issue
Covers indirect disclosure explicitly - a 'chasing a weird bug' post, a commit message, or a livestream of the fix all count as disclosure
Names coordinated disclosure as the governing norm: the report stays private and details are published only once a fixed version exists
Instructs that once the fixed release ships, the release notes say plainly that it contains a security fix so downstream users know to upgrade rather than treating it as an optional patch
Permits the full writeup only after the fixed version is available
Applies the pre-publish question about exposing an unfixed weakness directly or by hint
States that a disclaimer, vagueness or omitting the word 'security' does not neutralize the problem
Classifies this as a hard block rather than a grey zone needing a judgement call or a recorded decision
Does not offer an obfuscated, delayed-detail or anonymized version of the bug hunt as a compromise

evals.prompt: We're four engineers at Tessellate, selling a self-hosted observability agent, about 60 paying teams on v2. Marketing wants a public roadmap page with quarters attached: Q2 v3 storage engine, Q3 managed cloud, Q4 v3 GA. Their argument is that enterprise buyers need to see we're serious and have a future. I'm the CTO, something about it bothers me and I can't articulate it. Tell me whether to do it.
evals.expected_output: A response that names the Osborne effect, rejects the dated entries for unshipped work, allows direction and sequencing without dates, specifies non-commitment language if a roadmap ships anyway, and answers the enterprise-buyer motive with operational evidence instead.
expectations: Names the Osborne effect as the specific risk of announcing an unshipped successor while still selling the current version
Explains the mechanism: buyers defer or cancel purchases of the shipping product once its successor is announced
Cites the Osborne Computer Corporation 1983 precedent - prototype successors announced, dealers cancelled orders for the shipping machine, sales collapsed
Gives the rule: publish direction and sequencing, and attach dates only to work already shipping
Rejects the page as drafted, specifically the dated Q2/Q3/Q4 entries for unshipped work

If a roadmap is published anyway, requires explicit non-commitment language modelled on GitHub's public roadmap: subject to change, not a commitment guarantee obligation or promise, and not to be relied on for purchasing decisions
Classifies roadmap dates as a grey zone requiring a decision recorded in the charter rather than a reflex
Warns that a roadmap detailed enough to be useful can read as competitor intelligence
States that missed dates cost more credibility than the announced feature earns
Answers the enterprise-buyer motive with evidence a company evaluator actually uses - release cadence, response times, security handling, maintenance capacity - instead of dated promises

evals.prompt: I run Fernbrook, a habit-tracking app, solo, $9,400 MRR. I post a revenue chart every month on X and honestly that has been my entire growth channel for two years. In the last six weeks three near-identical apps have appeared, one of them shipped with my exact onboarding copy. Everyone in my group chat says execution beats ideas and nobody can copy me. Do I stop posting numbers or is that just fear talking?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to settle the objection with the classic rebuttal, presents the current dated disagreement from both sides without declaring a winner, states the share-the-journey-not-the-playbook working rule, and converts the stop decision into a written pre-commitment.
expectations: Does not settle the objection with the classic 'execution beats ideas / nobody can copy the you in your product' rebuttal alone
Presents the disagreement as currently open and does not declare either side to have won
Gives Arvid Kahl's 2026 reassessment, attributed and dated: agentic coding tools turn a publicly described architecture and feature set into a working competitor in days
States Kahl's specific claim that the old safety threshold of $20-30K MRR has collapsed to zero
Gives the counter-position that the barrier to a clone was always getting strangers to trust it, so distribution and trust remain the moat
States the working rule: share the journey and the reasoning, and keep the operational playbook, the exact architecture and the specific growth levers out of public writing
Distinguishes describing what you built (safe) from describing precisely how it wins (handing over a plan)
Notes that the working rule holds under either reading of the disagreement

Points at the four documented stop conditions (belittling by larger companies, copy and clone risk, the number reading as bragging past some size, the number no longer being a personal milestone once others are on the team)
Treats stopping as a pre-commitment written down in advance rather than a reaction to the current month
Warns that withdrawing a published number is itself a second public event, read defensively regardless of the real reason, not a neutral reset
Requires deciding now what stays published if the revenue chart is retired, rather than letting the chart go silently stale

evals.prompt: Northgate Data - we sell a data-lineage tool, average contract around $48k a year. Our buyers are platform engineering leads at insurance and banking companies who then have to push it through procurement and a security review. We closed $610k ARR last year, up from $240k. Our founder wants that number published monthly on the website, his reasoning being that it proves we're real and growing fast. I run marketing and I have to give him an answer this week.
evals.expected_output: A response that identifies the company-adoption reader, warns that a small honest revenue number invites a vendor-viability objection in procurement, redirects to operational evidence, and requires consent plus a written stop condition before any number is published.
expectations: Identifies the reader as a company-adoption evaluator who must convince an internal approver, not an individual adopter choosing for themselves
Warns that revenue disclosure can backfire here: a small honest number next to an incumbent invites a vendor-risk or vendor-viability objection during procurement
Recommends operational evidence over financial disclosure for this audience, naming release cadence, response times, security handling and maintenance capacity
Places the recommendation on the disclosure ladder explicitly, at operational metrics rather than financials
States that published financials cannot be unpublished and that the company would be measured against that baseline permanently
States the rule that a metric should only be published if the company will keep publishing it while it declines
Names what is identical regardless of which reader it is: the security boundary, the consent rules and the cadence math
Does not propose publishing ARR with added context, framing or a growth-rate emphasis as a way to neutralize the vendor-risk objection
Asks whose consent is required before publishing company numbers - co-founders, investors, customers - rather than assuming the founder can decide alone
Requires a stop condition written before the first publication, including what stays published if the revenue number is later withdrawn

evals.prompt: I'm a backend engineer, six years in, trying to move into a staff role or land a DevRel job next year. My plan is to build in public. I've got a small side project, a Terraform linter with about 200 stars, and I want to post every single day about what I'm learning as I go - Rust, parser design, whatever I hit that week. Where do I start, and what should the first month look like?
evals.expected_output: A response that separates the three practices conflated under one name, identifies this as learning in public with the attribution, redirects toward a personal practice that keeps the project's numbers out of it, and challenges the daily cadence before designing anything.
expectations: Distinguishes the three practices conflated under the same name: build in public, 'release early, release often', and 'learning in public'
Identifies what this user described as learning in public - a career practice about an individual developer's skill and reputation
Attributes learning in public to Shawn Wang (2018)

Attributes 'release early, release often' to Eric Raymond (1997) and describes it as an engineering practice aimed at code quality and contributor recruitment, needing a release process rather than a content cadence
Describes build in public itself as a marketing practice aimed at building an audience that becomes users, contributors or sponsors
Directs the user toward a personal-brand practice rather than designing a project practice around the Terraform linter
Advises keeping the project's numbers out of the personal practice
Confirms which practice is wanted before designing any cadence, disclosure rung or platform mix

evals.prompt: Backstory: I maintain sift, a log-parsing tool, and last year I publicly committed to a Friday update every week. Made it to week 11, then a contract job ate my life. That was five months ago and the last post still says 'more soon'. Two people have opened issues asking whether the project is dead. It isn't - I've merged about thirty PRs since then, I just stopped writing. I want to start again in January. How do I do that without it collapsing again?
evals.expected_output: A restart plan built on one honest catch-up post and a cadence explicitly lower than the weekly one that broke, anchored to releases, sized to the worst month, with a pause rule written in advance.
expectations: Prescribes a single catch-up post covering the gap honestly - what shipped, what stalled, what changed - rather than quietly resuming as if nothing happened
Sets the restart cadence explicitly lower than the weekly cadence that broke
States that restarting at the previous frequency usually reproduces the same collapse
Names the failure mode of the weekly-log pattern: the streak becomes the obligation and one miss feels terminal
Explains that an announced gap costs nothing while an unannounced one reads as abandonment and shows up in other people's adoption decisions
Re-sizes the new cadence against the worst month rather than a good one
Recommends a release-anchored cadence given the roughly thirty merged pull requests, because the material already exists
Writes a pause rule into the plan now, with both the trigger and the sentence that announces the drop
Does not prescribe more frequent posting, a public streak, or an accountability commitment as the fix
States that the silence rather than the inactivity produced the 'is it dead' perception, since the project kept shipping throughout

evals.prompt: Corvid Labs, we build a CI caching service. We've been doing build-in-public posts for seven months, two a week, mostly written by me and our founding engineer. We're at 14.2k followers across two platforms and engagement looks fine. Our CFO asked me on Monday to show what it has returned and I genuinely don't know how to answer her. What should I be measuring, and what do I tell her?
evals.expected_output: A measurement answer that concedes attribution is narrative and promises signals not proof, instruments click-through per channel rather than followers, judges quarterly against the primary outcome with an explicit signal-to-ignore, and gives the self-set pass condition plus its two failure branches.
expectations: States that attribution in this practice is narrative rather than instrumented, and promises signals rather than proof
Backs that honesty with the documented case of Alex Turnbull, whose Groove transparency blog is a canonical success story and who later admitted he never looked at a metric for three years
Rejects follower count explicitly as a measure of whether the practice works
Prescribes instrumentation from day one regardless: tagged links, privacy-friendly analytics, and click-through to signup or waitlist tracked per channel
Sets the review period at quarterly and states that the practice compounds too slowly to read week to week
Judges the practice against the primary outcome chosen at the start rather than a generic engagement dashboard
Pairs each outcome with a signal to ignore - stars, followers, impressions or reach - not only with a signal that counts
Diagnoses a large audience that does not convert as missing channel-offer fit rather than insufficient effort, attributed to Jason Leow
Gives the reallocation rule: if engagement-to-signup conversion stays near zero across two to three months, treat the practice as a community and accountability tool and reallocate the time
States the pass condition as self-set rather than an industry benchmark, and notes that no public dataset gives realistic build-in-public conversion rates
Gives the three-part quarterly pass condition: at least one named outcome moved, the cadence was met, and no boundary rule was breached

Gives both failure branches in the right order - cadence met but nothing moved for two consecutive quarters means change the rung or the surface rather than posting more; cadence missed means cut the cadence before changing anything else

evals.prompt: Rough morning. We shipped 4.2 of our SDK on Tuesday and it double-charged webhook retries for anyone on the async client with a custom retry policy. About 300 accounts affected, one customer got billed six times over for a day. It's fixed in 4.2.1 as of an hour ago and refunds are going out. Our support lead wants to email only the affected accounts and say nothing publicly. Our CEO wants a blog post. We've published openly for two years. What do we do, and if we post, what does it actually say?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to publish first and publicly, in one place, structured impact then cause then systemic change, with no individual blame, a stated next-update date, and a rule for handling replies and later corrections.
expectations: Recommends publishing it publicly and first, on the company's own terms, rather than emailing affected accounts only
States that the same news extracted or surfaced by someone else is far more expensive than publishing it yourself
Specifies the order: impact on the reader first, then cause, then what changes systemically, and explicitly rejects the reverse order
Requires the impact stated in terms a reader can check against their own account or installation
Requires saying what is not yet known and when the next update lands, then meeting that date
Prohibits blame of individuals, vendors or contributors, and requires a systemic description instead
Publishes once, in full, in one place, with replies linking back to it rather than relitigating the same point across threads
Instructs to answer the strongest objection once, in public, and never to argue the same point across many threads
Requires any later correction to be published at the same prominence as the original claim, never as a reply to a stale post
Distinguishes live-incident status updates, which belong on a status page, from analysis, which belongs in a postmortem once causes are confirmed
Requires the post to name a systemic change to the release or testing process, not only the patched version

evals.prompt: Solo founder here, Palisade Analytics, privacy-first product analytics, 40 paying customers. Everything I've published for a year lives on my X account - the roadmap is a pinned thread, I post numbers there, people ask support questions in the replies. I've drafted one milestone post about hitting 40 customers and I want to push the identical text to X, LinkedIn, Hacker News, r/SaaS and my newsletter this week. Sanity check me before I hit send.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the identical cross-post with per-channel rewriting, a named owned anchor surface with the social accounts demoted to amplifiers, the specific failure mode of each proposed channel, and a verifiability requirement on the customer count.
expectations: Rejects posting identical text across the five surfaces and requires rewriting per channel
States that different post types are different genres rather than one asset reshaped for each platform
Names one anchor surface the project owns - changelog, blog or newsletter - and demotes the social channels to amplifiers pointing back to it
Gives the reason owned surfaces matter: the archive survives a platform decaying or an account being lost
Flags living entirely on one social platform as a failure mode: no archive, no search surface, and one account suspension away from losing the whole practice
Warns that Hacker News and Reddit actively punish marketing language, hype and unverifiable metrics
Warns that LinkedIn punishes casual indie tone and naked metric-flexing
Advises using only channels the founder actually reads and where this audience already evaluates tools
Notes that no single post carries a funnel because of the short half-life of a social post, so cadence and repurposing do the work

If a post half-life figure is cited, gives the measured median of roughly 80 minutes from Twitter impression data (Pfeffer, Matter and Sargsyan, ICWSM 2023) and does not present the 18-24 minute engagement-proxy figure as the measured one, explaining that the two measure different things
Requires a published customer count to come from a source the reader can verify rather than an unverifiable screenshot
Requires public posts to link back to the owned artifact rather than duplicating it, so a correction has one place to be made
Flags the roadmap living as a pinned social thread as a problem separate from the cross-posting question

evals.prompt: Since I started posting weekly about mesh-router (my Rust service-mesh sidecar) six months ago, stars went from 900 to 6.8k and open issues went from 14 to 180. Contributors are still basically me plus one person who shows up occasionally. My DMs are full of feature requests. I've also been publishing my sponsorship income, which is now about 310 EUR a month, and two separate people have told me I 'owe' them fixes because of it. I don't want to stop posting but this is not sustainable.
evals.expected_output: A response that reads issue volume outpacing contributor count as the signal to pause posting and fix artifacts, publishes availability and scope, routes requests off DMs, and connects the published income directly to the entitlement being experienced.
expectations: Reads issue volume growing faster than contributor count as the named signal to pause posting and fix an artifact instead of publishing more
Prescribes publishing availability and scope where arriving readers see them - README and community health files - rather than only responding faster
Routes feature requests off DMs and into a public channel so each answer is reusable
Declines out-of-scope work by pointing at the written scope rather than deciding case by case
Connects the published sponsorship income directly to the entitlement the user is experiencing: published maintainer income invites entitlement from unpaid users
Requires pairing any income disclosure with a published statement of what maintenance the money does and does not buy
Treats stars as proving nothing about adoption and pairs or replaces them with contributor, download or retention movement
Does not recommend posting more, or asking the audience for contributors, as the primary fix for the support load
Frames the practice as a budget rather than a growth channel, because the attention it buys arrives as issues, questions and opinions in the same place the maintainer ships from
Offers a cadence reduction or pause that is announced in a sentence rather than a silent fade-out
